mcqs.question: What's the strongest overall plan for warming a cache after a restart?
options: Only pre-populate hot keys ahead of time; ramping traffic in is unnecessary once you've pre-warmed
Only ramp traffic in gradually; pre-warming ahead of time is redundant work
Wait for the cache to fill naturally with no change to the deployment process
Pre-populate hot keys ahead of time when there's lead time, and ramp traffic in gradually regardless, as a safety net
mcqs.explanation: The two strategies are complementary, not alternatives: pre-warming only works for planned restarts with lead time, and ramp-in is what protects you the rest of the time, including whatever the pre-warm missed or an unplanned crash with zero notice. Relying on only one leaves a gap the other would have covered.

mcqs.question: Why does warming only the top 1000 keys by request volume, instead of the whole dataset, still meaningfully protect the database?
options: Warming any keys before traffic arrives always causes stale reads
The whole dataset must be warmed for a warming plan to have any effect at all
Access patterns are skewed, so a small set of hot keys absorbs the large majority of real traffic
Warming keys before traffic arrives requires taking the database offline
mcqs.explanation: Real traffic concentrates on a small fraction of keys — warming just the top N by volume covers most of what will actually be requested, without the cost of warming millions of rarely-read rows. Pre-warming doesn't inherently cause staleness (it's a snapshot read, same as any cache fill), doesn't require warming everything, and doesn't need the DB taken offline.

mcqs.question: The interviewer points out the entire cluster restarts at once, not one node at a time. What actually fixes this?
options: Making the pre-warming snapshot larger so it covers this case too
Rolling restarts — restarting nodes a few at a time so part of the cluster always stays warm and serving traffic
Gradual traffic ramp-in, since it doesn't require advance notice
This scenario doesn't need a fix since it can't happen in a well-run cluster
mcqs.explanation: Both pre-warming and ramp-in assume some part of the cluster is warm and can absorb load while the rest catches up — a simultaneous full-cluster restart breaks that assumption entirely, since there's no warm capacity left anywhere. The actual fix is at the deployment level: never restart the whole fleet at once. A bigger snapshot or ramp-in alone doesn't address a fully cold cluster, and this absolutely does happen in practice with naive deploy scripts.

mcqs.question: What's the actual flaw in assuming "the cache will just fill up naturally fast enough" after a cold start?
options: It skips the arithmetic — if a warm cache normally absorbs 95% of reads, a cold cache means the database instantly sees roughly 20x its usual load, which it may not survive long enough to "fill up"
It's a valid assumption as long as traffic stays exactly constant during the fill-up window
It's fine because most caches fill up within a few milliseconds regardless of size
It's only wrong for caches larger than a few gigabytes
mcqs.explanation: The belief ignores the multiplier: a database sized for a 5% miss rate is not sized for 100% of read traffic, and that gap is exactly what a cold cache exposes it to. Traffic doesn't need to spike for this to be dangerous — normal traffic against an unprepared DB is already the failure mode. Fill-up time depends on dataset size and traffic volume, not a universal few milliseconds.
